title: The passion fruit in Indonesia
titleCn: 印尼百香果种植与产业

paragraphs.text: A passion fruit production in Indonesia.
Listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.

Today, I'll be discussing the significance of passion fruit farming in Indonesia, its influence on the economy, and how it compares with other countries that grow the fruit commercially. Let's begin with the growing conditions. You might assume that tropical fruit, like passion fruit, would flourish in coastal areas, but in fact, that's not the case. In Indonesia, passion fruit can only grow successfully at a certain altitude. Specifically, it needs to be planted in areas that are at least eight hundred meters above sea level. This elevation offers the right balance of sunlight and cooler air, which are essential for healthy growth.

Although some people believe that fertile valleys would be ideal for farming, the passion fruit actually performs better in mountainous terrain with less humidity. Over the last few years, there's been a noticeable increase in the volume of passion fruit being harvested. Many farms in Western Java, in particular, have reported significantly higher yields compared to the past. This change hasn't come about randomly. It's largely the result of improved cultivation techniques, access to better seedlings, and some degree of government assistance for small farmers.

Of course, some regions have experienced declines due to poor management, but nationally, the trend has been largely positive. And while it may seem like the output has simply held steady, the actual statistics show a marked rise in yield.

That being said, it's important to note that this increase hasn't been consistent across the board. In some areas, the weather has had a negative impact on production. Passion fruit is quite delicate and doesn't respond well to sudden shifts in climate. Extended periods of rain or unseasonal dry spells can both reduce the number of viable fruits on a vine.

While it's true that pests can affect some crops, insects are not considered a major concern for passion fruit in this region. Likewise, irrigation isn't the main issue, as most plantations receive adequate water supply through natural rainfall. Now let's take a brief look at Kenya, where an interesting development has taken place. Until a few years ago, their passion fruit season was fairly limited. But thanks to recent innovations in greenhouse farming and irrigation control, fruits can now be grown throughout the whole year. This is a big step forward for farmers there, as it allows for more stable income and continuous export opportunities, regardless of the season. While some improvements in Kenya have focused on boosting fruit size or reducing the harvest time, those have been secondary. The year-round cultivation remains the most impactful breakthrough.
In contrast, New Zealand faces a few hurdles with its passion fruit exports.

One particular problem is the appearance of color fading. Even though the fruit may still taste fine after being stored for a certain time, its skin can lose its vibrant color and look less appealing. Exporters often find that by the time the fruit reaches overseas markets, it looks less fresh, which can affect its sale price.

Contrary to what some might think, the issue isn't really about insufficient supply. In fact, production levels are adequate. And while delays in transportation can cause issues for some fresh goods, that's not the main reason for consumer dissatisfaction here.

Now, moving on to consumer preferences. In Western countries like Germany and the UK, passion fruit is becoming increasingly popular. One of the main reasons for this is that it is additive-free. In other words, the fruit doesn't need artificial colorings or preservatives to stay fresh or taste good. This natural quality appeals to health-conscious consumers who prefer cleaner labels and fewer chemicals in their food.

Some buyers may also be drawn to its sweetness or its relatively large size, but those characteristics are more secondary. The absence of chemical additives is what really sets it apart in the market.

Despite this rising demand, Indonesian exporters have sometimes faced shortages. In recent years, one major issue has been unstable price levels. Prices tend to fluctuate frequently, making it hard for farmers to plan their planting seasons with confidence. When prices are low, they may decide not to grow the fruit at all, and when prices rise, it's often too late in the season to start.
It's not due to young trees either, as most plantations are well established and mature.
And labor availability, while important, hasn't posed a major problem in these regions.
Another country we should revisit is New Zealand. When we compare their situation to Kenya, we find a different limitation.
While Kenya can cultivate year-round, New Zealand's growing season is much more restricted.
In fact, the plant period is short, only running from February through to July. This gives farmers a narrow window for harvesting, which limits the amount they can produce in a single year.
Although some have pointed to a lack of equipment as a challenge or even poor soil condition in certain areas, these are not the main barriers in this case.

Despite these challenges, passion fruit farming continues to bring value to many economies. In Indonesia, while some of the harvest is sold in local markets, it's estimated that over ninety-five percent of the produce is exported, particularly to regions like South America, where it's used in juices, desserts, and even cosmetics. Finally, let's consider the socioeconomic effects of this industry. Because passion fruit farming is relatively labor-intensive, it can provide jobs for a sizable workforce, particularly in rural communities where employment opportunities are often limited. And aside from creating work, the expansion of the industry can improve the use of land. Many of the highland regions where passion fruit is grown were previously underdeveloped or used inefficiently.
Now, they're being turned into productive agricultural zones, boosting both local income and national exports.
